misconceptions.statement: The longest chord can be any chord passing near the middle of the circle.
misconceptions.why: Students see 'middle' chords as roughly the same length and do not link longest chord to the diameter.
misconceptions.fix: The diameter, which passes through the centre, is the longest chord. Any chord not through the centre is shorter than the diameter.

probe.question: Chord AB passes very close to but not through the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Can AB be 10 cm long?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is almost the diameter so it can be 10 cm.

misconceptions.root_belief: nearly the same means exactly the same

misconceptions.statement: Equal angles at the centre means nothing about chord lengths, since longer arcs always give longer chords.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on arc length intuition and ignore the congruent triangle link between angle and chord.
misconceptions.fix: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, and the converse is also true. Chord length depends on the angle at the centre in the same circle.

probe.question: Chords PQ and RS of the same circle subtend 60 degrees each at the centre. Compare PQ and RS.
probe.wrong_answer: Cannot say; they may differ in length.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works only in one direction

misconceptions.statement: The line from the centre to a chord always bisects the chord.
misconceptions.why: Students remember 'bisects' but forget the line must be perpendicular.
misconceptions.fix: Only the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. A slanting line from the centre to a chord does not hit its midpoint.

probe.question: O is the centre and OM meets chord AB at M with angle OMA = 70 degrees. Is AM = MB?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a line from the centre bisects the chord.

misconceptions.statement: The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees only when the triangle is isosceles.
misconceptions.why: Students see the textbook figure with the third point at the top middle and take that symmetric picture as the rule.
misconceptions.fix: For any point on the circle, the angle subtended by a diameter is 90 degrees. Its position on the semicircle does not matter.

probe.question: AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle close to A, so AC is much shorter than BC. What is angle ACB?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not 90 degrees because the triangle is not isosceles.

misconceptions.root_belief: Theorem holds only for the typical symmetric diagram
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom observation of textbook diagram effects

misconceptions.statement: Any two opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal.
misconceptions.why: Students mix this with the property of parallelograms, where opposite angles are equal.
misconceptions.fix: In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles add up to 180 degrees. They are equal only when each is 90 degrees, as in a rectangle.

probe.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 70 degrees. Find angle C.

misconceptions.root_belief: Opposite angles in quadrilaterals are always equal
misconceptions.source_hint: geometry misconception studies on quadrilateral properties

misconceptions.statement: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the adjacent interior angle.
misconceptions.why: Students pick the wrong interior angle because they do not link 'opposite' to the vertex across the quadrilateral.
misconceptions.fix: The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle. It is supplementary to the adjacent interior angle.

probe.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, side AB is extended to E and angle ABC = 100 degrees. What is the exterior angle CBE?
probe.wrong_answer: 100 degrees, the same as the adjacent angle ABC.

misconceptions.root_belief: Exterior angle equals the angle next to it

misconceptions.statement: Angles in the same segment are equal even when they stand on different chords.
misconceptions.why: Students remember only 'angles in the same segment are equal' and forget the same chord or arc condition.
misconceptions.fix: Angles are equal only if they stand on the same chord or arc and lie in the same segment.

probe.question: P and Q lie on the major arc. Angle APB stands on chord AB and angle CQD stands on chord CD, where CD is longer than AB. Are the two angles equal?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both angles are in the same segment so they are equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: Theorems apply without checking their conditions

misconceptions.statement: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circle for any two angles on the same chord.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the double rule without checking that the circle angle lies on the major arc and the centre angle is the one on the same arc.
misconceptions.fix: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circle only when both stand on the same arc. A point on the minor arc sees the reflex angle at the centre.

probe.question: Chord AB subtends an angle of 80 degrees at the centre O. What is the angle at a point P on the minor arc AB?

misconceptions.root_belief: Double rule works regardless of which arc
misconceptions.source_hint: research on circle theorem application errors

misconceptions.statement: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at any point where it touches or crosses the circle.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the perpendicularity as a property of every line near the radius and forget the contact point condition.
misconceptions.fix: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to its point of contact only. A secant cuts the circle at two points and is not perpendicular to the radius.

probe.question: A line cuts the circle at A and B. Is it perpendicular to radius OA?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a line touching the circle at A is always perpendicular to OA.

misconceptions.root_belief: Words tangent and secant are interchangeable

misconceptions.statement: Two tangents from an external point are equal only if the point is at the same distance as the centre of the circle from each point of contact.
misconceptions.why: Students think the two lengths depend on the angle between tangents and not on the right-angled triangles formed with the radius.
misconceptions.fix: Tangents from an external point are always equal, because the two right triangles share the hypotenuse OP and have equal radii.

probe.question: PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O. If PA = 7 cm and angle APB is 40 degrees, what is PB?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot be found because the angle is not 60 degrees.

misconceptions.root_belief: Equality needs a special angle or symmetric picture

misconceptions.statement: Two tangents can be drawn from a point inside a circle.
misconceptions.why: Students carry the rule 'two tangents from a point' from the external case to every position of the point.
misconceptions.fix: From an external point there are two tangents, from a point on the circle exactly one, and from an interior point none.

probe.question: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point inside it?

misconceptions.root_belief: A rule for one case holds for all cases

misconceptions.statement: Any four points that form a quadrilateral always lie on one circle.
misconceptions.why: Students see circles as always available and do not realise that three points fix a circle, so the fourth must be checked.
misconceptions.fix: A circle passes through any three non-collinear points, but a fourth point lies on it only if the opposite angles add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: In quadrilateral ABCD angle A = 80 degrees and angle C = 70 degrees. Is ABCD cyclic?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every quadrilateral can be inscribed in a circle.

misconceptions.root_belief: Every figure can be inscribed in a circle
